In Nick Campbell, Dafydd Gibbon & Daniel Hirst (eds.), Proceedings of Speech Prosody 7 (Dublin, 20-23 May 2014), 487-491. ISCA. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2014-85. Open PDF: https://www.isca-archive.org/speechprosody_2014/patino14_speechprosody.pdf
catalog_locator: sec. 2.2 'Syllable structure', p. 487 right column (bottom) continuing to p. 488 left column top, example (1); supporting: sec. 2.4 p. 488 and sec. 5 p. 489
catalog_quote: Last but not least, lexical stress functions as a culminative, hierarchical, delimitative and rhythmic unit [9], falling regularly on the penultimate syllable. Typologically, Nahuatl has a polysynthetic structure with the possibility of the object and even some modifiers being incorporated to the verb root. Structures above five or six syllables are not the most frequent, but they are not unusual either. In such words secondary stress is found. According to Kager’s classification [9], these synthetic structures in Morelos Nahuatl are typical of a bound or limited system, which is also non-sensitive to quantity, and it assigns stress from right to left, producing left-oriented, i.e. trochaic feet: [nik.ˌkʷah.kʷal.ˌt͡ɬaʃ.kal.ˈma.ka] (1) /ni-k-kʷaːhkʷal-t͡ɬaʃkal-maka/ 1SG.SUJ-3SG.OBJ-beautiful-tortilla-give.PRES 'I give him/her beautiful tortillas.' ... All three acoustic correlates (intensity, duration, and fundamental frequency or F0) signal, to a greater or lesser extent, the location and prominence level of primary stress, secondary stress, and lexical stress throughout the sentence. As such, the only constant acoustic correlate of stress is F0 [6].
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable; vowel length does not attract stress (quantity-insensitive). Whorf 1946 (Milpa Alta/Tepoztlán, snippet-reconstructed, p. 369) says the same: 'Words over one syllable have primary accent on the penult'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Velázquez Patiño: in long polysynthetic words (over 5-6 syllables) secondary stress is assigned right-to-left in binary trochaic feet, e.g. [nik.ˌkʷah.kʷal.ˌt͡ɬaʃ.kal.ˈma.ka]; primary vs secondary difference is only relative (p. 489). Whorf 1946 p. 370 (snippet): secondary accent on an ultima ending in -C and on the first syllable of a long word.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for native words. Whorf 1946 p. 381 (snippet): final accent in Hispanized place names only, 'in Aztec they are accented on the penult'. Loanword stress not discussed by Velázquez Patiño.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress; data from read sentences and elicited spontaneous utterances of Cuentepec speakers (one young male for vowel study; 3 speakers for intonation); all three correlates (intensity, duration, F0) signal stress but F0 is the only constant one (p. 488); stress interacts with a phonemic vowel length contrast that is 'not robust' in Cuentepec.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source describes the Cuentepec (municipio Temixco) variety of Morelos Nahuatl, squarely within more1259 / ISO nhm. The secondary corroboration (Whorf 1946) describes Milpa Alta (Mexico City) with notes on Tepoztlán, Morelos; Glottolog files Whorf's sketch under more1259, but Milpa Alta itself is geographically outside Morelos. Tetelcingo Nahuatl (tete1251, nhg), also in Morelos, is a separate languoid and was not used.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penult, trochaic penultimate stress) and as Velázquez Patiño 2014 for Cuentepec (Morelos). Adds detail: loud stress + pitch pattern on the penult, secondary accent on C-final ultima / initial syllable of long words / alternating syllables, and a three-way loud/medial/weak stress grading. Caveat: Whorf's primary object is Milpa Alta (Distrito Federal), with Tepoztlan (Morelos) only in notes; Glottolog links 'Nahuatl (Milpa Alta) at WALS' to more1259, so the assignment follows Glottolog/WALS.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Polysyllabic words carry primary accent (loud stress plus one of two tone patterns) on the penultimate syllable; secondary accent on a consonant-final ultima, on the first syllable of a long word, and on alternating syllables before the primary accent. Hispanized place names with Spanish final stress are penult-accented in Aztec.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: secondary accent on (1) an ultima ending in a consonant, (2) the first syllable of a long word, (3) alternate syllables before the primary accent (the snippet is cut after 'alternate syllables before the'); Whorf also distinguishes loud-, medial- and weak-stressed syllables (vowel section: 'Medial-stressed vowels are slightly shorter than loud-stressed').
new_statements.exceptions: None found in the recovered snippets beyond the note that Spanish final accent in Hispanized place names does not apply in Aztec. Whorf's 'two varieties of tone-pattern' means the primary accent has an associated pitch component ('stress accent with associated pitch differences'); the full description of the 'normal tone-pattern' varieties (beginning 'words ending .') was not recoverable from snippets.
new_statements.identity_note: Whorf 1946 describes the Milpa Alta dialect (Milpa Alta, Distrito Federal / Mexico City), with notes on Classical Aztec and on Tepoztlan (Morelos); it is filed under more1259 because Glottolog's more1259 page links 'Nahuatl (Milpa Alta) at WALS'. The existing catalog statement (Velázquez Patiño 2014) is for Cuentepec (Temixco), Morelos. Pharao Hansen 2016 (already held by the project from the earlier reading) is silent on Hueyapan stress and its only stress remark concerns Zongolica (Veracruz) Nahuatl, not this language.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penult: penultimate stress) and as Velazquez Patino 2014 (Cuentepec, Morelos); adds the loud-stress-plus-tone characterisation and the three secondary-accent sites. no open full copy of the 1946 volume exists online that this machine can reach.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Milpa Alta Aztec (with Tepoztlan, Morelos, said to pattern alike) every word of more than one syllable carries primary accent (loud stress plus a pitch pattern) on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary accent on (1) a consonant-final ultima, (2) the first syllable of a long word, (3) alternate syllables counting back from the primary accent, where a short open syllable is 'hurried' and does not count and two such in succession count as one.
new_statements.exceptions: Hispanized Aztec place names take Spanish final accent; 'in Aztec they are accented on the penult' (p. 381, snippet held from the earlier reading). Monosyllables fall outside the rule ('words over one syllable').
new_statements.identity_note: Whorf's object is the Nahuatl of Milpa Alta (Distrito Federal / Mexico City), with notes on Tepoztlan (Morelos) and Classical Nahuatl; Glottolog files the reference under Morelos Nahuatl (more1259, ISO nhm) and WALS 'Nahuatl (Milpa Alta)' is linked to more1259. The catalog's deciding source describes Cuentepec (Temixco, Morelos). Both are central-dialect Nahuatl varieties with the pan-Nahuatl penultimate stress.
